context: Al-Humazah is Makkan, from the years when mockery was Quraysh’s cheapest and most constant weapon against the believers. Some commentators name individuals behind the revelation, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, but the chains for a specific occasion are not firm, and the surah itself refuses to narrow: waylun li-kulli, woe to every humazah lumazah, every gesture-mocker and word-slanderer, whoever fits the description in any age.

The surah drew the anatomy of a familiar Makkan figure: rich enough to sneer, counting and recounting his wealth, half-believing the pile made him permanent. For the mocked believers, many of them enslaved or poor, it reframed their humiliation completely: the laughter aimed at them was evidence in a case being prepared, and the fire waiting for unrepentant contempt was described with a precision found nowhere else, a fire that climbs to the hearts, the very organ the mockery came from.
name_story: The surah is named for al-humazah, the habitual fault-finder who wounds with gesture and glance, paired in its first verse with lumazah, the tongue-slanderer. Some early books also cite it by the fire it unveils, al-Hutamah, the Crusher, so its names hold both the crime and the sentence.

movements.note: Woe is pronounced on every needling mocker and slanderer, and the source of his confidence is named at once: wealth gathered and counted, counted again.
Yahsabu anna malahu akhladah: he half-believes his wealth has made him immortal, the quiet creed underneath every sneer.
Kalla, by no means: he will be hurled into al-hutamah, and to the question, what will make you know what it is, comes the answer: the kindled fire of Allah.
A fire that mounts to the hearts, closing over its people in stretched-out columns: the sentence fitted exactly to the organ where contempt lived.

themes.d: Humazah and lumazah are intensive forms: not a man who once mocked, but a man whose mockery has become his craft and comfort.
The recounted pile is a liturgy of self-reassurance. The surah exposes the arithmetic underneath arrogance: he thinks the total is a lifespan.

themes.t: The fire that finds the heart
themes.d: Tattali’u ala al-af’idah: uniquely in the Quran, this fire is described reaching the hearts, justice tracing the crime to its source.
Ma aghna anhu maluhu: the currency he trusted is not accepted at the one gate that matters, a refrain this surah shares with its neighbors.

heart: Al-Humazah read slowly forces a double honesty. The first is social: the reciter checks himself for the small tools of the humazah, the raised eyebrow, the imitation of someone’s accent, the message forwarded with a laughing remark, because the surah’s woe is written on the habit, not the century. The second honesty is financial: yahsabu anna malahu akhladah, he supposes his wealth has made him last. Almost no one says that sentence aloud, and almost everyone has felt its warmth, the sense that enough saved, enough owned, is a wall against death. The surah calls the wall a supposition and knocks it through in one syllable, kalla.

Then the fire, and the detail that stays with every attentive reciter: it climbs to the hearts. The heart that looked down on Allah’s servants, the heart that leaned on the pile, is the address the punishment knows. The reader closes this surah gentler with people and looser with money, which is exactly the repentance it was sent to produce.

passages.why: Hear the woe pronounced on a habit our age has made effortless, mockery at a distance.
The unspoken creed of accumulation, said aloud once in the Quran so you can recognize it in yourself.
The most precise sentence in the surah: the fire that knows the way to the hearts.

connections.why: At-Takathur diagnoses the counting sickness in a whole society; Al-Humazah shows it concentrated in one condemned figure.
Al-Masad is the named case study: a real mocker of the Prophet ﷺ whose wealth and earnings availed him nothing.

virtue.text: No authentic hadith attaches a specific recitation reward to Al-Humazah, and it needs no certificate: it stands as the Quran’s permanent verdict on wealthy contempt, and its recital is its own admonition.
